title: What Prepositions Do: A Teacher's Overview
brief: Define prepositions as words that link a noun or pronoun to another element in the sentence, expressing relationships of time, place, movement, manner, and more. Explain that English prepositions are a closed lexical class — new ones are rarely coined — and that the same word can serve multiple functions (e.g., 'on' in time, place, and movement contexts). Introduce the three main categories this unit covers (time, place, movement) and flag dependent prepositions as a fourth area. Use original example sentences to illustrate each category briefly, setting up the sections that follow. Do not discuss phrasal verbs or prepositional phrases as clause constituents — those are reserved for other units.

title: Prepositions of Time: At, On, In and Beyond
brief: Explain the core time prepositions 'at', 'on', and 'in' using a specificity framework: 'at' for precise points (at noon, at midnight, at 3:45), 'on' for days and dates (on Friday, on 12 March, on New Year's Day), and 'in' for longer periods (in April, in 2019, in the nineteenth century, in the morning). Then address prepositions that fall outside this trio — 'during', 'for', 'since', 'by', 'until', and 'within' — with original example sentences showing how each marks a distinct temporal relationship. Highlight common learner errors such as 'in Monday' or 'at the morning' and explain why the specificity framework helps but does not eliminate all confusion. Do not discuss aspect or tense — those belong to other units.

title: Prepositions of Place: Locating People and Things
brief: Cover the principal prepositions used to describe static location: 'at', 'on', and 'in' revisited for place (at the station, on the shelf, in the garden), then extend to 'above', 'below', 'beside', 'between', 'among', 'opposite', 'behind', 'in front of', 'next to', and 'underneath'. Use original example sentences that contrast easily confused pairs, such as 'between' (two reference points: between the bank and the café) versus 'among' (an undifferentiated group: among the trees). Explain the 'at/on/in' place distinction through scale: 'at' for a point or address, 'on' for a surface or line, 'in' for an enclosed or bounded space. Note that 'at' and 'in' can both appear with buildings but carry different meanings (at the hospital = the general location; in the hospital = inside it). Invent all examples.

title: Prepositions of Movement: Direction and Path
brief: Distinguish movement prepositions from place prepositions by showing that movement prepositions describe a trajectory rather than a static position. Cover 'to', 'into', 'onto', 'through', 'across', 'along', 'past', 'around', 'up', 'down', 'out of', and 'away from' with original example sentences for each. Contrast pairs that learners conflate: 'to' (destination: she walked to the park) versus 'into' (entry: she walked into the building); 'across' (surface crossing: they swam across the river) versus 'through' (passing inside a space: they hiked through the forest). Address the 'go home / arrive home' zero-preposition pattern as a genuine exception worth flagging explicitly. Keep the focus on single-word and two-word prepositions; do not treat phrasal verbs.

title: Dependent Prepositions: Verbs and Adjectives That Demand a Partner
brief: Explain that dependent prepositions are prepositions required by a specific verb or adjective whose choice cannot be predicted from general rules — the combination must be learned as a unit. Provide original examples of verb + preposition pairs (apologise for, insist on, rely on, result in, consist of, agree with, differ from) and adjective + preposition pairs (afraid of, responsible for, interested in, familiar with, capable of, disappointed with). Show how the same verb can take different prepositions with different meanings (argue with someone / argue about something / argue for a position). Explain that learners who try to translate from their first language or apply logic frequently produce errors (e.g., 'explain me' instead of 'explain to me', 'interested about' instead of 'interested in'). Emphasise that these combinations resist rule-based explanation and must be encountered repeatedly in context.

title: Teaching Prepositions: Chunks, Patterns, and Classroom Practice
brief: Argue that because prepositions — especially dependent ones — resist simple rules, the most effective classroom approach treats them as lexical chunks to be learned in context rather than as isolated words governed by a single formula. Describe three practical techniques: (1) presenting prepositions inside fixed phrases from the start (at the weekend, on time, in a hurry) so learners store the whole chunk; (2) using pattern drills that contrast minimal pairs (interested in / good at / afraid of) to build automatic retrieval; and (3) encouraging learners to keep a collocation notebook where new verb + preposition and adjective + preposition combinations are recorded in full example sentences rather than as bare word lists. Suggest a simple classroom activity: give learners a short paragraph with prepositions blanked out, ask them to predict the missing words, then discuss why certain answers feel right or wrong — using that uncertainty as a teaching moment about the arbitrary nature of dependent prepositions. Do not make claims about research or studies.
